A faint dashed circle of that radius surrounds the central node, and two points are joined exactly when they lie within the radius of each other, so edges fill in as the radius grows (1, 6, and 10 edges)." width="100%"} Places `n` nodes uniformly at random in the unit hypercube and connects nodes whose distance is at most the value provided in `radius=`. This creates spatial networks where nearby points are more likely to be connected. Every pair of new nodes is checked, and an edge is added exactly when the distance between their positions (measured with the Minkowski `p_norm=` metric) is less than or equal to `radius=`. The edges are unweighted. Each node's position is stored in its label, so the geometry can be recovered later. The new nodes get the next available node IDs; existing nodes are left untouched and never connected to the new ones. In a directed graph each edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. Random geometric graphs are useful for modeling: - wireless networks (nodes in radio range) - social networks (geographically close individuals) - biological networks (spatially proximate cells) - ad-hoc networks and sensor networks ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes to add. `n=0` adds nothing. [radius]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum distance for edge creation. Nodes within this distance are connected. Must be non-negative. Larger values give denser graphs; in the unit square with Euclidean distance the expected degree is roughly `n * pi * radius^2` (a bit less because of edge effects near the boundary). [dim]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of dimensions for the unit hypercube (default `2`). Use `2` for planar graphs, `3` for spatial networks. In higher dimensions points are farther apart on average, so a larger `radius=` is needed for the same density. Must be at least `1`. [p_norm]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minkowski distance parameter (default `2.0` for Euclidean). Common values are `1.0` (Manhattan) and `2.0` (Euclidean); for the same `radius=`, smaller values give a smaller neighborhood and so fewer edges. Must be positive. Only finite values work correctly at present: `float("inf")` (Chebyshev distance) connects every pair. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator that places the nodes. The same `seed=` with the same `n=` and `dim=` always gives the same positions. If `None` (default), positions differ on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `radius=` is negative, `dim=` < `1`, or `p_norm=` <= `0`, or if a position label is already used in the graph (e.g. adding the same seeded graph twice); nothing is added in that case. ::: ## Properties {.doc-properties} - **Edge direction**: none in an undirected graph; in a directed graph, edges point from the earlier-created node to the later one. - **Spatial embedding**: nodes have positions in `[0, 1]^dim`. - **Node labels**: position stored as a JSON array with six decimal places, e.g., `"[0.234000, 0.567000]"`; `json.loads()` turns it back into a list of floats. - **Local clustering**: high clustering due to geometric proximity. - **Threshold behavior**: graph connectivity exhibits phase transition as radius increases past a critical threshold. ## Complexity {.doc-complexity} - Time: `O(n²)` for distance comparisons (naive algorithm) - Space: `O(n × dim)` for positions plus O(edges) for graph ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes are scattered uniformly at random in the unit square, and only those within `radius=` of each other get connected: ::: {#dab5c7e0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=100, radius=0.2, seed=23 ) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (100, 527) ``` ::: ::: Each node's label records its coordinates, so the spatial layout stays inspectable after construction. Here is the position of the first node: ::: {#efe7ad45 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_label_from_id(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` '[0.541348, 0.246466]' ``` ::: ::: The labels are JSON arrays, so `json.loads()` turns them back into coordinates, e.g. to compute positions for plotting: ::: {#89bdbb38 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json positions = { nid: json.loads(graph.get_label_from_id(nid)) for nid in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None) } positions[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [0.541348, 0.246466] ``` ::: ::: The graph's connectivity has a sharp threshold. With `100` nodes, small radii leave the graph split into pieces, and somewhere between `0.2` and `0.25` it becomes connected: ::: {#876523eb .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} [ (r, ec.Graph().add_random_geometric_graph(n=100, radius=r, seed=23).is_connected()) for r in (0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [(0.1, False), (0.15, False), (0.2, False), (0.25, True)] ``` ::: ::: Raising `dim=` embeds nodes in 3D space instead of 2D, which is useful for modeling physical or volumetric proximity. Each label then holds three coordinates: ::: {#2246f9c9 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} spatial_graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=50, radius=0.3, dim=3, seed=123 ) spatial_graph.count_edges(), spatial_graph.get_label_from_id(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (88, '[0.853472, 0.167583, 0.335330]') ``` ::: ::: Switching to `p_norm=1.0` measures distance with the Manhattan (taxicab) metric instead of Euclidean distance. With the same seed (so the same node positions) and the same radius, the Manhattan neighborhood is a diamond that fits inside the Euclidean circle, so fewer pairs are connected: ::: {#db2ed7ce .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} manhattan_graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=100, radius=0.25, p_norm=1.0, seed=23 ) euclidean_graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_random_geometric_graph( n=100, radius=0.25, seed=23 ) manhattan_graph.count_edges(), euclidean_graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (531, 803) ``` ::: :::
